Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|1|0.source_text: No Malay explainer for Stage 1 units: explainers and rubrics are in Japanese or English (Sam, 11 Nov 2026). Select 日本語 or English.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|2|0.source_text: Five sentence patterns from Kata-Kata, each with question-and-answer examples. Read the examples in pairs first, then the explanation.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|1.source_text: 1. A: Selamat pagi, Puan Aini.  B: Selamat pagi, Encik Tanaka.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|2.source_text: 2. A: Selamat tengah hari, Cik Mei Ling.  B: Selamat tengah hari, Encik Rahman.
target_spans: Selamat tengah hari, Cik Mei Ling.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|3.source_text: 3. A: Selamat petang, Pak cik.  B: Selamat petang, Encik.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|4.source_text: 4. A: Selamat malam, Mak cik.  B: Selamat malam.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|5.source_text: 5. A: Selamat datang, Encik Tanaka!  B: Terima kasih, Puan.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|6.source_text: Explanation: Selamat plus a time word makes a greeting: pagi (morning), tengah hari (around midday), petang (mid-afternoon to dusk), malam (night). Add a title and then the name. A title alone is also polite: Selamat pagi, Puan.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|7.source_text: 説明：Selamat に時間帯の語をつけるとあいさつになります。pagi（朝）、tengah hari（昼ごろ）、petang（午後〜夕方）、malam（夜）。そのあとに敬称と名前を言います。敬称だけでも丁寧です：Selamat pagi, Puan.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|8.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: Titles work like さん, but they come before the name: Encik Tanaka. Selamat malam covers both こんばんは and おやすみなさい. こんにちは is split in two: Selamat tengah hari around midday, Selamat petang later.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|9.source_text: 日本語との比較：敬称はさんに似ていますが、名前の前に来ます。Selamat malam は「こんばんは」と「おやすみなさい」の両方です。「こんにちは」は二つに分かれます：昼ごろは Selamat tengah hari、午後は Selamat petang。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|12.source_text: 1. A: Apa khabar, Encik Tanaka?  B: Khabar baik, terima kasih.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|13.source_text: 2. A: Apa khabar, Puan Aini?  B: Baik, terima kasih.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|14.source_text: 3. A: Apa khabar, Pak cik?  B: Baik. Terima kasih.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|15.source_text: 4. A: Selamat pagi, Kakak. Apa khabar?  B: Khabar baik.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|16.source_text: Explanation: Apa khabar? (literally "what news?") asks how someone is. Answer Khabar baik ("good news") or just Baik. Add the title at the end to make it personal.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|17.source_text: 説明：Apa khabar?（直訳「どんな便り？」）は相手の様子をたずねます。答えは Khabar baik（よい便り）か Baik だけでも大丈夫です。最後に敬称をつけると丁寧です。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|18.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: It is close to お元気ですか, but Malaysians use it more widely, for example with someone they have just met.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|19.source_text: 日本語との比較：「お元気ですか」に近いですが、初めて会った人にも使えるなど、もっと広く使われます。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|3|21.source_text: Pattern box: Khabar baik, terima kasih. (title) pula?

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|0.source_text: 1. A: Khabar baik, terima kasih. Puan pula?  B: Saya pun baik.
target_spans: Khabar baik, terima kasih. Puan pula?

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|1.source_text: 2. A: Baik, terima kasih. Encik pula?  B: Baik, terima kasih.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|2.source_text: 3. A: Khabar baik. Cik Mei Ling pula?  B: Saya pun baik, terima kasih.
target_spans: Khabar baik. Cik Mei Ling pula?

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|3.source_text: 4. A: Saya baik. Pak cik pula?  B: Pak cik pun baik.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|4.source_text: Explanation: pula turns the question back to the other person ("and you?"). pun after a word means "too": Saya pun baik = I am fine too. Use the person's title, not a word for "you". Older speakers often call themselves Pak cik or Mak cik.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|5.source_text: 説明：pula は質問を相手に返します（「あなたは？」）。pun は語のあとについて「〜も」の意味です：Saya pun baik＝私も元気です。「あなた」ではなく相手の敬称を使います。年配の人は自分を Pak cik・Mak cik と呼ぶことがよくあります。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|6.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: pun comes after the word it adds to, just like も: Saya pun ≈ 私も. pula? ≈ 〜は？ in あなたは？

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|7.source_text: 日本語との比較：pun は「も」と同じく語のあとに来ます：Saya pun≈私も。pula? は「あなたは？」の「は？」に近いです。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|10.source_text: 1. A: Maaf, tumpang tanya. Encik Tanaka?  B: Ya, saya Tanaka.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|11.source_text: 2. A: Maaf, tumpang tanya. Puan Aini?  B: Tidak. Saya Mei Ling.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|12.source_text: 3. A: Maaf, Pak cik. Tumpang tanya.  B: Ya?

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|13.source_text: 4. A: Maaf, Encik Rahman?  B: Ya, saya.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|14.source_text: 5. A: Terima kasih, Kakak.  B: Sama-sama.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|15.source_text: Explanation: Maaf is "sorry" or "excuse me". Tumpang tanya politely asks to ask something. Confirm with ya or deny with tidak (spoken: tak). Answer thanks with Sama-sama.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|16.source_text: 説明：Maaf は「すみません・ごめんなさい」。Tumpang tanya は「ちょっとお尋ねします」。確認は ya、否定は tidak（話し言葉では tak）。お礼には Sama-sama で答えます。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|17.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: Maaf, tumpang tanya ≈ すみません、ちょっとお尋ねします. But Japanese すみません can also mean thank you; in Malay, thanks is always terima kasih.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|4|18.source_text: 日本語との比較：Maaf, tumpang tanya は「すみません、ちょっとお尋ねします」に近いです。ただし日本語の「すみません」はお礼にも使いますが、マレー語のお礼は必ず terima kasih です。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|0.source_text: Pattern box: Saya minta diri dulu. Jumpa ___ !

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|1.source_text: 1. A: Saya minta diri dulu. Jumpa esok!  B: Jumpa esok. Selamat jalan!
target_spans: Saya minta diri dulu. Jumpa esok!

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|2.source_text: 2. A: Maaf, saya minta diri dulu.  B: Ya. Jumpa lagi!

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|3.source_text: 3. A: Jumpa nanti, Cik Mei Ling.  B: Jumpa nanti.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|4.source_text: 4. A: Selamat malam, Puan. Jumpa esok.  B: Selamat malam. Jaga diri!

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|5.source_text: 5. A: Terima kasih, Pak cik. Jumpa lagi!  B: Hati-hati, Encik!
target_spans: Terima kasih, Pak cik. Jumpa lagi!

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|6.source_text: Explanation: Saya minta diri dulu means "I will take my leave first". Jumpa + esok / lagi / nanti = see you tomorrow / again / later. Selamat jalan is said to the person leaving; Selamat tinggal to the person staying, and it sounds final.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|7.source_text: 説明：Saya minta diri dulu は「お先に失礼します」。Jumpa ＋ esok・lagi・nanti＝また明日・またね・あとで。Selamat jalan は出かける人に、Selamat tinggal は残る人に言います。Selamat tinggal は別れの響きが強い言葉です。

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|8.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: Saya minta diri dulu ≈ お先に失礼します. Careful: Selamat jalan is said by the person staying (≈ いってらっしゃい), not by the one who leaves.

Unit 1 · Pattern and grammar focus|5|9.source_text: 日本語との比較：Saya minta diri dulu≈お先に失礼します。注意：Selamat jalan は残る人が言う言葉（≈いってらっしゃい）で、帰る本人は言いません。

Unit 1 · Culture and word-origin note|2|.source_text: Read where the greeting words come from and how they are used (English and Japanese).

Unit 1 · Culture and word-origin note|3|.source_text: Selamat, the first word of most greetings, comes from Arabic salāma, "wellbeing". Selamat pagi is a wish: may your morning be well. Khabar is also Arabic and means "news", so Apa khabar? asks "what news?" and Khabar baik answers "good news".
Terima kasih joins terima, "receive", and kasih, "affection": you receive someone's kindness. Tumpang tanya pairs tumpang, "ride along", with tanya, "ask": you borrow a moment of someone's time.

Two goodbyes depend on who moves. Selamat jalan, "safe going", is said to the person leaving; Selamat tinggal, "safe staying", to the person who stays. Selamat tinggal sounds final, so everyday partings use Jumpa lagi or Jumpa esok.

Titles matter. Use Encik for a man, Puan for a married or senior woman and Cik for a young woman, before the name. A title on its own is the polite "you": Puan pula? Abang and Kakak, "older brother" and "older sister", are friendly titles for waiters, drivers and shop staff of about your age; Pak cik and Mak cik, "uncle" and "auntie", are for older people.
あいさつの最初の語 Selamat は、アラビア語の salāma（無事・平安）から来ています。Selamat pagi は「よい朝でありますように」という願いです。Khabar もアラビア語で「便り」の意味なので、Apa khabar? は「どんな便り？」、Khabar baik は「よい便り」です。
Terima kasih は terima（受け取る）と kasih（愛情）から成り、相手の好意を受け取るという意味です。Tumpang tanya は tumpang（相乗りする）と tanya（たずねる）で、相手の時間を少し借りる表現です。
別れのあいさつは、だれが動くかで変わります。Selamat jalan（無事に行って）は出かける人に、Selamat tinggal（無事に残って）は残る人に言います。Selamat tinggal は別れの響きが強いので、ふだんは Jumpa lagi や Jumpa esok を使います。
敬称も大切です。男性には Encik、既婚・年上の女性には Puan、若い女性には Cik を名前の前につけます。敬称だけで丁寧な「あなた」になります：Puan pula?。Abang・Kakak（兄・姉）は同年代の店員や運転手への親しい呼びかけ、Pak cik・Mak cik（おじさん・おばさん）は年上の人への呼びかけです。

■ What to listen for · 注意点
Title before the name; no Tanaka Encik. pun after the word. Selamat jalan from the person staying.
Final k as a catch, not a full く: baik, tidak. No vowel added after final consonants: Encik, not "enchiku".
Spoken tak only after tidak has been taught, and always labelled spoken.

Unit 1 · Pronunciation and spelling bloc.source_text: マレー語のつづりと発音はほぼ規則的です。日本語話者が注意したい音を練習し、最後に書き取りをします。
（日本語は下書きです。ネイティブ・スピーカーの確認待ち）
No Malay explainer for Stage 1 units: explainers and rubrics are in Japanese or English (Sam, 11 Nov 2026). Select 日本語 or English.
Malay spelling is close to regular. Practise the sounds Japanese speakers find tricky, then take a short dictation.
a, i, o are close to Japanese あ, い, お. u is rounder than う: Jumpa, Puan.
e has two sounds and the spelling does not show which. Weak e (like the a in "about"): selamat, petang, terima kasih, Encik.
Clear e (like え): esok. Learn each word with its sound.
e には二つの音があり、つづりでは区別しません。弱い e（あいまい母音）：selamat、petang。はっきりした e（え）：esok。
■ 2 · Consonants · 子音
c sounds like ち: Cik, Encik, Pak cik.
ng is one sound, as in "sing" (no ぐ after it): petang, tengah hari.
kh, from Arabic, is a soft sound from the back of the throat: khabar.
Final k is a catch in the throat, not a full く: baik, tidak, Pak cik, Mak cik.
r and l are different sounds: terima kasih, diri (tap the r); selamat, lagi, malam (tongue touches for l).
No extra vowel after a final consonant: maaf, not "maafu"; malam, not "maramu". Double aa in maaf is two syllables: ma-af.
ち・ん・のどの音などに注意。語末に母音を足さないこと。r と l は別の音です。
■ 3 · Read aloud in pairs · ペアで音読
pagi · petang · malam · esok
Encik · Cik · Pak cik · Mak cik
baik · tidak · maaf
terima kasih · selamat · lagi · diri
sama-sama · hati-hati (a repeated word is written with a hyphen)
Selamat berkenalan · khabar · Apa khabar?
■ 4 · Dictation · 書き取り
Your teacher reads eight words. Write them.
Check: is there a hyphen in a repeated word? Did you write ng, c and kh correctly?
Dictation (read twice): 1 pagi 2 malam 3 esok 4 baik 5 Encik 6 khabar 7 petang 8 sama-sama.
Unverified: these pronunciation notes are from general knowledge of standard Malaysian Malay, not checked against a reference. Sam to confirm before teaching.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|0.source_text: Pattern box: Nama saya ___ . / Ini ___ . Namanya ___ .

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|1.source_text: 1. A: Nama saya Rahman. Encik pula?  B: Nama saya Tanaka.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|2.source_text: 2. A: Ini kawan saya. Namanya Ali.  B: Selamat berkenalan, Ali.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|3.source_text: 3. A: Itu Cik Mei Ling?  B: Ya, itu Cik Mei Ling.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|4.source_text: 4. A: Nama awak Yuki?  B: Ya, nama saya Yuki.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|5.source_text: 5. A: Ini Encik Kumar. Namanya Kumar.  B: Selamat berkenalan, Encik Kumar.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|6.source_text: Explanation: Two nouns side by side make a sentence: Nama saya Tanaka (my name, Tanaka). There is no word for "is". saya after nama means "my". ini (this) is near you, itu (that) is further away. -nya on a noun means his, her or its: namanya = his or her name.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|7.source_text: 説明：名詞を二つ並べると文になります：Nama saya Tanaka。「〜です」にあたる語はありません。nama のあとの saya は「私の」。ini（これ・この）は近く、itu（それ・あれ）は遠く。名詞に -nya をつけると「彼の・彼女の・その」：namanya＝その人の名前。

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|8.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: Japanese also puts the owner first in 私の名前, but Malay puts it last: nama saya = name + me. No は, の or です are needed.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|9.source_text: 日本語との比較：日本語の「私の名前」とは逆に、マレー語は持ち主が後ろに来ます：nama saya＝名前＋私。「は」「の」「です」はいりません。

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|12.source_text: 1. A: Siapa nama encik?  B: Nama saya Kimura.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|13.source_text: 2. A: Siapa nama puan?  B: Nama saya Aini.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|14.source_text: 3. A: Itu siapa?  B: Itu Encik Rahman.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|15.source_text: 4. A: Siapa nama kawan awak?  B: Namanya Mei Ling.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|16.source_text: 5. A: Dia siapa?  B: Dia kawan saya.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|17.source_text: Explanation: siapa means "who". Malay asks for a name with "who": Siapa nama encik? The question word can also stay where the answer goes: Itu siapa? (that is who?). Use the title as "you" with people you do not know well.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|18.source_text: 説明：siapa は「だれ」。名前をたずねる時も「だれ」を使います：Siapa nama encik?。疑問詞を答えの位置に置いたままでもかまいません：Itu siapa?（あれはだれ？）。よく知らない相手には「あなた」の代わりに敬称を使います。

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|3|19.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: お名前は何ですか uses 何 (what), but Malay uses siapa (who). Like Japanese, the question word can stay in place: Itu siapa? ≈ あれはだれ？

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|0.source_text: 日本語との比較：「お名前は何ですか」は「何」ですが、マレー語は siapa（だれ）です。日本語と同じく、疑問詞をそのままの位置に置けます：Itu siapa?≈あれはだれ？

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|2.source_text: Pattern box: Saya orang ___ . Asal saya dari ___ .

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|3.source_text: 1. A: Encik orang Jepun?  B: Ya, saya orang Jepun. Asal saya dari Osaka.
target_spans: Ya, saya orang Jepun. Asal saya dari Osaka.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|4.source_text: 2. A: Puan orang Malaysia?  B: Ya. Asal saya dari Ipoh.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|5.source_text: 3. A: Kampung encik di mana?  B: Kampung saya di Sapporo.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|6.source_text: 4. A: Mereka orang Jepun?  B: Tidak, mereka orang Malaysia.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|7.source_text: 5. A: Apa negara asal awak?  B: Negara asal saya Jepun.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|8.source_text: Explanation: orang (person) + a country = nationality: orang Jepun, orang Malaysia. asal is origin and dari is "from". A yes/no question can be a statement said with a rising voice: Encik orang Jepun?

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|9.source_text: 説明：orang（人）＋国名で国籍になります：orang Jepun、orang Malaysia。asal は出身、dari は「〜から」。はい・いいえの質問は、文の終わりを上げて言うだけでもできます：Encik orang Jepun?

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|10.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: orang Jepun is built like 日本人 (Japan + person), but in the opposite order: person + Japan. A rising voice works like か.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|11.source_text: 日本語との比較：orang Jepun は「日本人」と同じ作りですが、順番が逆です（人＋日本）。文末を上げるのは「か」と同じ働きです。

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|13.source_text: Pattern box: ___ di mana? / Di mana ___ ?  (unit 2B adds di manakah)

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|14.source_text: 1. A: Kampung encik di mana?  B: Di Osaka.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|15.source_text: 2. A: Encik Rahman di mana?  B: Dia di Kuala Lumpur.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|16.source_text: 3. A: Di mana Cik Mei Ling?  B: Dia di Bangsar.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|17.source_text: 4. A: Kampung dia di mana?  B: Kampung dia di Johor Bahru.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|18.source_text: 5. A: Osaka di mana?  B: Osaka di Jepun.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|19.source_text: Explanation: di mana is "where": di (at) + mana (which place). Put it at the end, where the answer goes, or at the front. di is written as a separate word before a place: di Osaka.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|20.source_text: 説明：di mana は「どこ」：di（〜に）＋ mana。答えが入る文末に置いても、文頭に置いてもかまいません。di は場所の前に離して書きます：di Osaka。

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|4|21.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: Like どこ, di mana can sit where the answer goes. But di comes before the place (in Osaka), the reverse of 大阪に.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|5|0.source_text: 日本語との比較：「どこ」と同じく、答えの位置に置けます。ただし di は場所の前に来ます（di Osaka）。「大阪に」とは逆です。

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|6|0.source_text: Patterns are Kata-Kata frames ms-c02-f01, f02, f03 and f08 (taught here in its plain form di mana).

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|6|1.source_text: Teacher prompts: read each A line; the class gives the B line with their own facts.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|6|2.source_text: Check: Nama saya …, not Saya nama …; orang Jepun, not Jepun orang; di Osaka with di before the place.

Unit 2A · Pattern and grammar focus|6|3.source_text: Negating a noun (bukan) is a chapter 3 word: for now learners answer Tidak, saya orang Malaysia.

Unit 2A · Culture and usage note · Choos.source_text: 「あなた」の選び方、kami と kita、名前の習慣について読みます（英語と日本語）。
（日本語は下書きです。ネイティブ・スピーカーの確認待ち）
No Malay explainer for Stage 1 units: explainers and rubrics are in Japanese or English (Sam, 11 Nov 2026). Select 日本語 or English.
Read how to choose "you", the difference between kami and kita, and name customs (English and Japanese).

Malay has several words for "you", and choosing one is a social decision. With someone senior or someone you have just met, avoid a pronoun and use the title: Encik pula?, Puan orang Malaysia? Awak is the everyday "you" between colleagues of a similar age. Anda is formal and impersonal: you see it on signs, forms and adverts. Kamu is for children and juniors, and engkau or kau only for very close friends; it can sound rude to a stranger. Aku, the casual "I", goes with kau.

Two words mean "we". Kami leaves the listener out; kita takes the listener in. Kami orang Jepun tells a Malaysian that you and your friends are Japanese; Jom, kita jumpa nanti includes the person you are talking to. Japanese 私たち covers both.
Dia means both "he" and "she". For a respected person, such as a manager or a minister, Malaysians often say beliau.

Names follow their own customs. In most Malay names the second part is the father's name, not a family name, so the title goes with the person's own name: Encik Rahman. Chinese Malaysian names put the family name first, as Japanese names do.

マレー語には「あなた」にあたる語がいくつもあり、どれを選ぶかは人間関係の問題です。目上の人や初対面の人には代名詞を避け、敬称を使います：Encik pula?、Puan orang Malaysia?。Awak は同年代の同僚どうしのふだんの「あなた」。Anda は改まった、相手を特定しない言い方で、看板・書類・広告で見かけます。Kamu は子どもや目下の人に、engkau・kau はごく親しい友達だけに使い、知らない人には失礼に聞こえます。くだけた「私」の Aku は kau とセットです。
「私たち」も二つあります。Kami は聞き手を含まず、kita は聞き手を含みます。Kami orang Jepun はマレーシア人に「私たちは日本人です」と伝え、Jom, kita jumpa nanti は話している相手も含みます。日本語の「私たち」は両方を表します。
Dia は「彼」と「彼女」の両方です。マネージャーや大臣など敬意を払う人には beliau がよく使われます。
名前の習慣もさまざまです。マレー系の名前の多くは、後半が父親の名前で家族の姓ではありません。そのため敬称は本人の名前につけます：Encik Rahman。中華系マレーシア人の名前は、日本人と同じく姓が先です。
Sources: Kata-Kata card notes ms-c02-006 (avoid engkau with strangers) and ms-c02-007 (dia has no gender); ledger meanings L-0037 to L-0046.
Unverified: the name-custom paragraph is general knowledge, not from Sam's notes or a cited source. Sam to confirm.

Unit 2A · Teaching plan and answer key|3.source_text: Before Block A: Kata-Kata Sedia Kelas c02 (27 cards; frames ms-c02-f01, f02). Collect Tanya Cikgu questions.
After Block B: the unit 2A cards with spaced review. Before Block E: the Dunia scene "Sembang di pantri".
After Block D: Kata-Kata cards for unit 2B (work, home, family, pe- and -an). Planning figure: about 3 hours of Kata-Kata for this unit.
Hanashishou starts at A2: no link yet. Audio: teacher-read scripts only.
■ Block A · Words and patterns (45 min)
Goal: I can say my name and nationality and ask other people theirs.
0–5 Recall (Opener): greetings at four times. Expected: Selamat pagi …, Apa khabar?, … pula?
5–10 Tanya Cikgu. 10–20 Vocabulary: point at people for pronouns; ask which "you" for a manager (expected: the title).
20–40 Patterns 1 to 4: model the A lines; the class answers with their own facts. Prompt: "Is it Saya nama or Nama saya?" Expected: Nama saya.
40–45 First substitutions: Drill 2, items 1 to 3.
■ Block B · Drills and conversation (45 min)
Goal: I can ask who someone is and where they are from, and introduce a friend.
0–5 Recall: "Ask my name." Expected: Siapa nama puan? / Siapa nama encik?
5–25 Drill ladder in order, types 1 to 6. In drill 3, stress kami against kita.
25–40 Model conversation, gapped version, variant. 40–45 Pair rehearsal with real facts.
■ Block C · Listening and task (45 min)
Goal: I can follow a short round of introductions and read name tags.
0–5 Recall: "Introduce your partner." Expected: Ini … Namanya … Dia orang …
5–20 Listening: the table first, the script twice (on the listening key), then the questions.
20–30 Name tags: six questions, then the learner's own tag and sentences.
30–45 Task: role cards; announce the manager's arrival at minute 38.
■ Block D · Review and test (45 min)
Goal: I can check my introductions in a short test and say what I can do.
0–15 Mixed review: cumulative question-word drill, then chapter 1 greetings with the new questions.

Unit 2A · Teaching plan and answer key|4.source_text: 15–25 Unit test. 25–35 Self-check and feedback. 35–45 Preview the Kata-Kata unit 2B cards (work, home, family).
Goal: I can join a chat in the office pantry and choose the right word for "you".
0–5 Recall: "Which "you" on a form?" Expected: anda.
5–15 Scene listening: play or read the Kata-Kata Dunia scene "Sembang di pantri" (cards ms-d-pejabat-sembang-01 to 12).
15–30 Role-play the pantry chat in threes. 30–40 Free variation: an old friend arrives (Lama tak jumpa!).
40–45 Culture note on choosing "you". No Hanashishou link at A1.
■ What to listen for · 注意点
Nama saya (not Saya nama); orang Jepun (not Jepun orang); di before the place.
A title, not awak, with seniors. kami against kita. Spoken scene words are recognised first, then used only in chat.
Not taught: dari mana (chapter 7 in the ledger) and bukan (chapter 3); use Kampung … di mana? and Tidak, … instead.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|0.source_text: Pattern box: Saya kerja di ___ . Saya (job) . / Saya belajar di ___ .

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|1.source_text: 1. A: Encik kerja di mana?  B: Saya kerja di syarikat Jepun. Saya jurutera.
target_spans: Saya kerja di syarikat Jepun. Saya jurutera.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|2.source_text: 2. A: Puan kerja di mana?  B: Saya kerja di sekolah. Saya guru.
target_spans: Saya kerja di sekolah. Saya guru.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|3.source_text: 3. A: Cik pelajar?  B: Ya, saya belajar di Universiti Malaya.
target_spans: Ya, saya belajar di Universiti Malaya.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|4.source_text: 4. A: Apa kerja dia?  B: Dia pemandu.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|5.source_text: 5. A: Encik Rahman pengurus?  B: Ya, dia pengurus pejabat kami.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|6.source_text: Explanation: kerja di + a place says where you work; belajar di + a place, where you study. A job is just a noun after the person: Saya jurutera. Apa kerja …? asks someone's job. kerja is everyday speech; the formal written form is bekerja (a later chapter).

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|7.source_text: 説明：kerja di＋場所で働いている所、belajar di＋場所で勉強している所を言います。職業は人のあとに名詞を置くだけです：Saya jurutera。Apa kerja …? で職業をたずねます。kerja は話し言葉で、書き言葉では bekerja（後の章）です。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|8.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: di works like で in 会社で働いています. But Malay verbs never change: kerja covers 働く, 働いている and 働きます.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|9.source_text: 日本語との比較：di は「会社で働いています」の「で」に近いです。ただしマレー語の動詞は形が変わりません：kerja で「働く・働いている・働きます」を表します。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|11.source_text: Pattern box: Saya tinggal di ___ ( dengan ___ ).

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|12.source_text: 1. A: Encik tinggal di mana?  B: Saya tinggal di Mont Kiara.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|13.source_text: 2. A: Puan tinggal dengan siapa?  B: Saya tinggal dengan suami dan anak saya.
target_spans: Saya tinggal dengan suami dan anak saya.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|14.source_text: 3. A: Rumah cik di mana?  B: Rumah saya di Petaling Jaya.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|15.source_text: 4. A: Encik ada anak?  B: Ada. Anak saya belajar di sekolah Jepun.
target_spans: Ada. Anak saya belajar di sekolah Jepun.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|16.source_text: 5. A: Keluarga awak di mana?  B: Keluarga saya di Jepun.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|17.source_text: Explanation: tinggal di = live in. dengan = with. ada = have or there is; answer a yes/no question with Ada (yes) or Tidak ada (no). The owner comes after the thing: anak saya = my child, rumah cik = your house.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|18.source_text: 説明：tinggal di＝〜に住んでいる。dengan＝〜と一緒に。ada＝ある・いる・持っている。答えは Ada（はい）か Tidak ada（いいえ）。持ち主はもののあとに来ます：anak saya＝私の子ども、rumah cik＝あなたの家。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|19.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: dengan is close to と in 夫と住んでいます. ada covers ある, いる and 持っている.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|3|20.source_text: 日本語との比較：dengan は「夫と住んでいます」の「と」に近いです。ada は「ある」「いる」「持っている」をまとめて表します。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|0.source_text: Pattern box: Hobi saya ___ . / Saya suka ___ .

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|1.source_text: 1. A: Apa hobi encik?  B: Saya suka masakan Malaysia.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|2.source_text: 2. A: Puan suka makanan Jepun?  B: Ya, saya suka makanan Jepun.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|3.source_text: 3. A: Anak encik suka main?  B: Ya, dia suka main dengan kawan.
target_spans: Ya, dia suka main dengan kawan.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|4.source_text: 4. A: Awak suka kelas ini?  B: Ya, saya suka kelas ini!

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|5.source_text: 5. A: Isteri encik suka minuman Malaysia?  B: Tidak, dia tidak suka.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|6.source_text: 6. A: Apa hobi cik?  B: Hobi saya karaoke dan jalan-jalan.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|7.source_text: Explanation: suka (like) comes before a noun or a verb: suka masakan Malaysia, suka main. tidak suka = do not like. For Hobi saya ___, pick a word from the hobby word bank (karaoke, golf, hiking, oshikatsu …) or ask your teacher.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|8.source_text: 説明：suka（好き）は名詞や動詞の前に来ます：suka masakan Malaysia、suka main。tidak suka＝好きではない。Hobi saya ___ には趣味のことば（karaoke、golf、hiking、oshikatsu など）から選ぶか、先生に聞きましょう。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|9.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: In Japanese the thing you like comes first (料理が好き); in Malay it comes after suka: suka masakan. No が is needed.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|10.source_text: 日本語との比較：日本語は「料理が好き」と好きなものが先ですが、マレー語は suka のあとです：suka masakan。「が」はいりません。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|12.source_text: Pattern box: Di manakah ___ ? / Adakah ___ ? / Bolehkah ___ ?

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|13.source_text: 1. A: Di manakah pejabat encik?  B: Pejabat saya di Kuala Lumpur.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|14.source_text: 2. A: Siapakah nama encik?  B: Nama saya Tanaka.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|15.source_text: 3. A: Apakah nama syarikat puan?  B: Nama syarikat saya Sakura.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|16.source_text: 4. A: Adakah encik orang Jepun?  B: Ya, saya orang Jepun.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|17.source_text: 5. A: Bolehkah saya tanya?  B: Boleh.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|18.source_text: 6. A: Adakah Cik Mei Ling pelajar?  B: Tidak, dia jurutera.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|19.source_text: Explanation: -kah on a question word makes a formal question, used in writing, forms and announcements: Siapakah, Apakah, di manakah. Adakah opens a formal yes/no question; answer Ya or Tidak. Bolehkah asks politely if something is possible; answer Boleh or Tidak boleh. In everyday speech a rising voice is enough: Encik orang Jepun?

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|4|20.source_text: 説明：疑問詞に -kah をつけると、書き言葉・書類・アナウンスで使う改まった質問になります：Siapakah、Apakah、di manakah。Adakah は改まった「はい・いいえ」の質問を始め、答えは Ya か Tidak。Bolehkah は「〜してもいいですか・できますか」と丁寧にたずね、答えは Boleh か Tidak boleh。ふだんの会話では文末を上げるだけで十分です：Encik orang Jepun?

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|0.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: -kah works like か, but it sits on the word being asked about, not at the end. Bolehkah saya …? ≈ 〜してもいいですか.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|1.source_text: 日本語との比較：-kah は「か」に似ていますが、文末ではなく、たずねたい語につきます。Bolehkah saya …?≈「〜してもいいですか」。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|3.source_text: Pattern box: pe- + root = a person · root + -an = a thing

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|4.source_text: 1. A: Dia pelajar?  B: Ya, dia belajar di universiti.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|5.source_text: 2. A: Encik pekerja syarikat ini?  B: Ya, saya pekerja syarikat ini.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|6.source_text: 3. A: Ada soalan?  B: Ada. Bolehkah saya tanya?

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|7.source_text: 4. A: Ini jawapan awak?  B: Ya, ini jawapan saya.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|8.source_text: 5. A: Encik suka makanan Malaysia?  B: Ya, dan minuman Malaysia juga.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|9.source_text: Explanation: pe- turns a root into the person who does it: kerja → pekerja, ajar → pelajar, lawat → pelawat. With some roots the sound changes (pandu → pemandu, urus → pengurus): recognise these for now. -an turns a root into a thing: makan → makanan (food), soal → soalan (question), jawab → jawapan (b becomes p).

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|10.source_text: 説明：pe- は語根を「それをする人」にします：kerja→pekerja、ajar→pelajar、lawat→pelawat。音が変わる語（pandu→pemandu、urus→pengurus）は今は見て分かれば十分です。-an は語根を「もの」にします：makan→makanan（食べ物）、soal→soalan（質問）、jawab→jawapan（b が p に）。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|11.source_text: Japanese helps or misleads: This is like 〜者 or 〜手 (運転手) for people and 〜物 for things: makanan ≈ 食べ物, minuman ≈ 飲み物.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|5|12.source_text: 日本語との比較：人を表す「〜者・〜手」（運転手）、ものを表す「〜物」に似ています：makanan≈食べ物、minuman≈飲み物。

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|6|0.source_text: Patterns 1 to 4 are Kata-Kata frames ms-c02-f04 to f08. Box 5 is a grammar point (pe- and -an), not a frame.

Unit 2B · Pattern and grammar focus|6|2.source_text: Check: kerja di / tinggal di with di; owner after the thing (anak saya); suka before what is liked; -kah on the question word.

Unit 2B · Culture and word-origin note ·.source_text: pe- と -an による語の作り方、日常語と改まった語、-kah の使われ方を読みます（英語と日本語）。
（日本語は下書きです。ネイティブ・スピーカーの確認待ち）
No Malay explainer for Stage 1 units: explainers and rubrics are in Japanese or English (Sam, 11 Nov 2026). Select 日本語 or English.
Read how pe- and -an build words, which words are everyday and which formal, and where -kah questions are used (English and Japanese).

Malay builds new words from roots, and two of the first patterns are pe- and -an. pe- names the person who does something: kerja (work) gives pekerja (worker), ajar (teach) gives pelajar (student), lawat (visit) gives pelawat (visitor), lancong (tour) gives pelancong (tourist) and tani (farming) gives petani (farmer). With some roots the sound changes: pandu gives pemandu (driver) and urus gives pengurus (manager).

-an names the thing: makan gives makanan (food), minum minuman (drink), masak masakan (cooking), baca bacaan (reading material) and tulis tulisan (writing). jawab becomes jawapan, with b turning into p.
Learn these as words first; the rule helps you guess new ones on signs. Pelawat, for example, appears on visitor badges.

Two words have an everyday and a formal partner. Cikgu is the everyday word for teacher and guru the more formal one. Kerja is natural in speech; in formal writing it becomes bekerja, which you will meet with the ber- verbs in chapter 10.
The -kah questions sound formal. You will see Siapakah, Apakah and Adakah on forms and hear them in announcements and interviews. In conversation, a rising voice is enough.

マレー語は語根から新しい語を作ります。最初に学ぶ形が pe- と -an です。pe- は「それをする人」を表します：kerja（仕事）→pekerja（従業員）、ajar（教える）→pelajar（学生）、lawat（訪ねる）→pelawat（訪問者）、lancong（旅行）→pelancong（観光客）、tani（農業）→petani（農家）。音が変わる語もあります：pandu→pemandu（運転手）、urus→pengurus（マネージャー）。
-an は「もの」を表します：makan→makanan（食べ物）、minum→minuman（飲み物）、masak→masakan（料理）、baca→bacaan（読み物）、tulis→tulisan（書いたもの）。jawab は b が p に変わって jawapan になります。
まずは単語として覚えましょう。ルールを知っていると、看板の新しい語も推測できます。たとえば Pelawat は来客用の名札に書かれています。
日常語と改まった語の組もあります。先生は日常では Cikgu、改まると guru。Kerja は会話では自然ですが、改まった書き言葉では bekerja になり、第10章の ber- 動詞で学びます。
-kah の質問は改まって聞こえます。Siapakah・Apakah・Adakah は書類で見たり、アナウンスや面接で聞いたりします。会話では文末を上げるだけで十分です。

■ Block A · Words and patterns (45 min)
Goal: I can say where I work or study, where I live and who I live with.
0–5 Recall (Opener): name, nationality, hometown, then introduce a partner.
5–10 Tanya Cikgu. 10–20 Vocabulary: say a root, learners give the pe- or -an word. Expected: tulis → tulisan.
20–40 Patterns 1 to 5. Prompt: "Where do you work?" Expected: Saya kerja di …. Ask for a hobby word each learner needs and write it on the board as a personal word.
40–45 First substitutions: Drill 2, items 1 to 4.
■ Block B · Drills and conversation (45 min)
Goal: I can ask about someone's work, home, family and likes, formally and informally.
0–5 Recall: "Ask me formally where my office is." Expected: Di manakah pejabat puan?
5–25 Drill ladder, types 1 to 6. 25–40 Model conversation, gapped version, business-event variant. 40–45 Pair rehearsal.
■ Block C · Listening and task (45 min)
Goal: I can follow a self-introduction about work and family and read a self-introduction message.
0–5 Recall: "Who do you live with?" Expected: Saya tinggal dengan ….
5–20 Listening: table, script twice (on the listening key), questions. 20–30 Reading: Sato's message and the reply.
30–45 Task: role cards; switch to the formal interview at minute 37.
■ Block D · Review and test (45 min)
Goal: I can check my self-introduction in a short test and say what I can do.
0–15 Mixed review: cumulative question-word drill, formal then informal; recycle chapter 1 greetings at the start of each interview.
15–25 Unit test. 25–35 Self-check and feedback. 35–45 Preview Sedia Kelas c03.

5–15 Scene listening: play or read the Kata-Kata Dunia scene "Pagi di pejabat". 15–30 Role-play it in pairs.
30–40 Free variation: the boss is on leave (cuti) and a colleague is busy (sibuk). 40–45 Culture note. No Hanashishou link at A1.
Goal: I can fill in a self-introduction form and write a short self-introduction.
0–5 Recall the four questions (work, home, family, likes). 5–15 Read the model form and paragraph.
15–30 Learners fill in the form, then write five or six sentences. 30–40 Pairs swap and check with the checklist. 40–45 Read aloud.
■ What to listen for · 注意点
di before places; the owner after the thing; suka before what is liked; -kah on the question word, not at the end.
Hobby words are the learner's own: write them on the board as personal words, not as chapter vocabulary. Raised with Sam for the ledger.
pemandu and pengurus are recognise-only. The office words from "Pagi di pejabat" are for recognition first.

Unit 3A · Culture and usage note|3|0.source_text: In this unit, a quantity and an identifying number are deliberately treated as different tasks. A price or age is normally read as a complete quantity: for example, the pieces for the tens and units have to be kept in their proper order. A telephone number, however, can be read digit by digit. The classroom uses invented strings rather than asking learners to disclose a real personal number. The teacher should ask learners to say whether the digits represent a quantity, an age, or a code before deciding how to read them.

Unit 3A · Culture and usage note|3|1.source_text: Kata-Kata card ms-c03-011 explicitly notes that sepuluh is built from the one-unit prefix and the tens element; card ms-c03-012 gives the corresponding note for sebelas. The cards also introduce seratus, seribu and sejuta as standard number forms. These word-building observations are taken from the cards, not independent etymological claims. The aim is to make adult learners recognise the recurring structure while keeping irregular forms visible. Students should be able to read a price even when they cannot yet explain every part of its spelling.

Unit 3A · Culture and usage note|3|2.source_text: When recording information in a Malaysian classroom or office, ask for a repeat when an important digit is unclear. The speaker may group digits for convenience, but the listener must check the full sequence. This is a communication skill rather than a claim that one grouping style is universal. Use imaginary names and numbers in class, and let learners decline to share personal information. Japanese comparisons on this sheet are teaching drafts awaiting a native review.

No Hanashishou A1 scene. Listening uses the printed teacher script, not an audio file.
■ Block A · Words and patterns (45 min)
Goal: I can read numbers to one million and state an age.
0–5 Recall: chapters 1 and 2 (greeting, name, origin). 5–10 Tanya Cikgu questions.
10–20 core vocabulary, with recognition and revision categories kept separate.
20–40 the four or five pattern boxes, Q&A first, rule second. 40–45 first substitutions.
■ Block B · Drills and conversation (45 min)
Goal: I can ask and answer about ages and fictional phone digits.
0–5 Recall first pattern without notes. 5–25 six drills in section 14 order.
25–40 model conversation then gaps then changed-facts variant. 40–45 pair rehearsal.
■ Block C · Listening and task (45 min)
Goal: I can hear, confirm and write digits on a class form.
0–5 Recall two number sentences. 5–20 teacher-read listening, two readings.
20–30 six reading questions and writing. 30–45 role-play; change the plan mid-way.
■ Block D · Review and test (45 min)
Goal: I can retrieve the number patterns and check my accuracy.
0–15 mixed recall with cumulative question words including berapa, adakah and bolehkah.
15–25 low-stakes unit test; 25–35 self-check and correction; 35–45 Kata-Kata preview.
■ Block E · Dunia scene (45 min)
Goal: I can recognise numbers and queue-ticket words at a bank.
0–5 recall. 5–15 teacher-read Dunia scene. 15–30 pairs enact the scene.
30–40 change the situation and speak freely; 40–45 usage/culture discussion.
■ What to listen for · 注意点
Contrast a complete number with digit-by-digit reading.
Keep all identifying information fictional and check pronunciation of zero.

Unit 3B · Culture and usage note|3|0.source_text: The everyday classroom distinction between wang and duit deserves careful handling. Kata-Kata card ms-c03-022 describes wang as the standard word for money and duit as an everyday word. For this course, present wang first and explicitly mark duit as conversational vocabulary; do not imply that both have the same register. The card for beli notes that the root is used in speech while the full formal written active form is outside this stage. Learners can use the taught root in a simple buying exchange without being asked to construct productive me- verbs prematurely.

Unit 3B · Culture and usage note|3|1.source_text: Prices in Malaysian ringgit may include sen. A learner needs to hear the whole amount, not just its first number, and to distinguish an amount to pay from an amount returned as change. During a practice transaction the teacher should give the customer an explicit amount of fictional cash and ask both partners to calculate the expected baki. The numbers on this sheet are invented for teaching, not observed shop prices or price recommendations. Learners should check whether the price applies to one item or a group rather than assuming a unit without asking.

Unit 3B · Culture and usage note|3|2.source_text: The market setting is suitable for a second layer of listening. The Kata-Kata Dunia scene introduces produce and bargaining language. Those scene words are displayed separately as recognition vocabulary, because the core objective of this unit is to ask, pay, and confirm. Role-play a calm correction when the change does not match the amount paid. The teacher may accept a short, grammatical confirmation instead of requiring a long explanation. The Japanese comparison material is provisional and needs a native-speaker review.

Goal: I can ask a price and say an amount in ringgit and sen.

10–20 core vocabulary, with recognition and revision categories kept separate.

■ Block B · Drills and conversation (45 min)
Goal: I can pay with cash or card and confirm the change.
0–5 Recall first pattern without notes. 5–25 six drills in section 14 order.
25–40 model conversation then gaps then changed-facts variant. 40–45 pair rehearsal.
■ Block C · Listening and task (45 min)
Goal: I can understand a short market transaction and read a price list.
0–5 Recall two number sentences. 5–20 teacher-read listening, two readings.
20–30 six reading questions and writing. 30–45 role-play; change the plan mid-way.
■ Block D · Review and test (45 min)
Goal: I can check transaction language and arithmetic in a low-stakes test.
0–15 mixed recall with cumulative question words including berapa, adakah and bolehkah.
15–25 low-stakes unit test; 25–35 self-check and correction; 35–45 Kata-Kata preview.
■ Block E · Dunia scene (45 min)
Goal: I can recognise words in a morning-market scene.
0–5 recall. 5–15 teacher-read Dunia scene. 15–30 pairs enact the scene.
30–40 change the situation and speak freely; 40–45 usage/culture discussion.

Standard wang precedes everyday duit; sahaja precedes spoken saja.

Unit 3C · Culture and usage note|3|0.source_text: Ordinal numbers help speakers organise repeated visits and ordered choices. Kata-Kata card ms-c03-036 explicitly warns that pertama, not a mechanically created first ordinal, is the ordinary first-place expression. Cards ms-c03-037 to ms-c03-039 supply attested further ordinals. The teacher can contrast satu with pertama and dua with kedua without inventing a new derivation. When discussing which visit or attempt a person means, learners should repeat the entire ordinal after hearing it rather than simply agreeing.

Unit 3C · Culture and usage note|3|1.source_text: Fractions, decimal values and percentages answer different questions. A half-kilogram quantity is not the same thing as a fifty-percent discount, even though the fractions may be mathematically related. Use one written fictional label at a time and have the listener identify whether it names a share, a mass, a dimension, or a price reduction. Kata-Kata card ms-c03-044 gives dua perpuluhan lima for a 2.5 decimal, and card ms-c03-045 gives a fifty-percent example. These are card notes, not a claim about how every merchant speaks. This unit does not yet introduce classifier rules, which belong to chapter 8.

Unit 3C · Culture and usage note|3|2.source_text: The measurement vocabulary gives a useful introduction to the attested nouns ketinggian, kepanjangan, kelebaran and kedalaman. They are recorded as chapter 3 terms. Avoid telling students that any adjective can be changed with paired prefix and suffix: this lesson only practises the listed forms. In the writing task, ask for a clear unit after each number and for an explicitly fictional price when a price appears. This prevents learners from confusing metres with centimetres and full prices with discounted prices. The Japanese notes are still draft translations and require native review.

■ Block A · Words and patterns (45 min)
Goal: I can say ordinal positions, common fractions and percentages.
0–5 Recall: chapters 1 and 2 (greeting, name, origin). 5–10 Tanya Cikgu questions.
10–20 core vocabulary, with recognition and revision categories kept separate.
20–40 the four or five pattern boxes, Q&A first, rule second. 40–45 first substitutions.
■ Block B · Drills and conversation (45 min)
Goal: I can ask and answer about quantities and dimensions.
0–5 Recall first pattern without notes. 5–25 six drills in section 14 order.
25–40 model conversation then gaps then changed-facts variant. 40–45 pair rehearsal.
■ Block C · Listening and task (45 min)
Goal: I can read an order and write a simple measurement list.
0–5 Recall two number sentences. 5–20 teacher-read listening, two readings.
20–30 six reading questions and writing. 30–45 role-play; change the plan mid-way.
■ Block D · Review and test (45 min)
Goal: I can distinguish ordinal, fraction, percent and dimension forms.
0–15 mixed recall with cumulative question words including berapa, adakah and bolehkah.
15–25 low-stakes unit test; 25–35 self-check and correction; 35–45 Kata-Kata preview.
■ Block E · Dunia scene (45 min)
Goal: I can recognise remaining bank and post-office words.
0–5 recall. 5–15 teacher-read Dunia scene. 15–30 pairs enact the scene.
30–40 change the situation and speak freely; 40–45 usage/culture discussion.
■ What to listen for · 注意点
Do not introduce chapter 8 productive classifiers.
Keep paired prefix and suffix restricted to attested chapter 3 measure nouns.
